title: Evidence Harvest Orchestrator - Operator Proposal
content:
Purpose
This proposal describes the design for an Evidence Harvest Orchestrator (EHO) — a Kubernetes operator + light control plane to coordinate collectors across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments, produce canonical control evidence artifacts, and stream/sink validated audit events to SIEMs. The EHO fills gaps in our current collectors by: centralizing lifecycle, enforcing RBAC v2 scope rules for evidence capture, and adding cryptographic integrity checks and idempotent delivery semantics for SIEM exports.

Problem statement / Motivation
- We have multiple collectors (agent, log-forwarders, ingest-sidecar) with inconsistent output schemas, partial control mapping, and no single lifecycle for evidence tied to a control.
- Existing export flows can duplicate events or lose context across retries.
- Enterprise customers require tamper-evidence (signatures/HMACs) and proof chains for control evidence in audits.
- RBAC v2 introduces scoped shadows (e.g., read-only audit view vs evidence-granular view) — collectors must honor policy boundaries and redact when necessary.

Goals
1) Operator-managed collectors: deploy/update collectors, coordinate discovery, and perform rolling config updates with canaries.
2) Canonical evidence envelope: standardized audit schema + provenance fields + integrity materials (hashes, signatures).
3) Policy enforcement: integrate RBAC v2 policy engine to gate data capture, transform, and export.
4) Reliable SIEM/export: at-least-once delivery with deduplication keys and delivery receipts; support Splunk, Elastic, Datadog, and S3 snapshot backup.
5) Observability & test harness: per-control metric surface and replay tooling for regression testing evidence pipelines.

High-level architecture
- Kubernetes operator (EHO): watches a new CRD (EvidenceHarvest) to control collector topology, retention, and export policies.
- Collector sidecars/agents: lightweight adapters (fluent-bit, vector, or a built-in Go collector) that normalize local logs to the canonical audit schema and attach evidence envelopes.
- EHO control plane: policy enforcer (RBAC v2 client), signer service (integrates with KMS), dedupe store (redis/etcd), and export adapters.
- Long-term store: immutable S3 buckets for snapshots (WORM-like), with per-tenant prefixes and lifecycle rules.

EvidenceHarvest CRD (conceptual)
- apiVersion: security.redwood.ai/v1alpha1
- kind: EvidenceHarvest
- metadata:
    name: payment-service-controls
- spec:
    namespaceSelector: { matchNames: ["payments-prod"] }
    controlBindings: ["control-PCI-DSS-10-1","control-ACCESS-3"]
    collectors:
      - type: sidecar
        configRef: payment-sidecar-v1
    exportSinks: ["splunk-prod","s3-archive"]
    signerKeyRef: kms:/projects/redwood/keys/evidence-signing
    retentionDays: 400
    redactRulesRef: rbv2/redact/payment-service

Notes about the CRD: it couples a control group to a set of collectors and sinks so every piece of evidence can be traced back to a control binding and policy that allowed its capture.

Canonical audit envelope (required fields)
- event_id: uuidv4
- timestamp: ISO8601 UTC
- service: logical service id (payments-service)
- resource: { type, id }
- action: string (e.g., token:create, key.read)
- actor: { id, principal_type, role }
- result: { status, http_status, error_code? }
- trace_id / request_id: propagate from upstream if present
- control_id: canonical control id(s) this event maps to
- control_version: snapshot of control config when event captured
- provenance: { collector_id, collector_version, node_id, region }
- integrity: { algo: "SHA-256", hash: hex, signature: base64 (optional) }
- redaction: array of fields removed or masked with reason
- original_payload: base64 (optional; only if retention policy allows and RBAC permits)

Transformation rules and mapping
- Each collector provides a mapping file that maps local log attributes to the canonical envelope. The operator validates the mapping during rollout.
- A small rule engine (Lua or WASM) allows controlled enrichments (add trace links, normalize durations) but operator enforces sandboxed libraries so no exfil of raw payloads.

RBAC v2 enforcement points
1) Capture-time gating: EHO queries RBAC v2 policy for the harvesting scope — if the principal driving the collector lacks permission for certain attributes, the operator applies redaction rules before the event leaves the host.
2) Export-time gating: separate RBAC check for sink usage (e.g., only audit-team role can receive raw original_payload).
3) Admin operations: rolling restarts, signer key rotation, and S3 lifecycle changes require admin or compliance-operator role.

Integrity and tamper-evidence
- Local producers compute event-level hash (SHA-256) and attach to envelope.
- Operator's signer service periodically signs batches (daily) with an HSM/KMS-backed key, producing a signed manifest linking to daily snapshot(s).
- Retention snapshots stored in S3 are WORM-like (object lock for regulated customers).
- Proof chaining: each daily manifest includes previous_manifest_hash to make an append-only chain for auditors.

Deduplication and idempotency
- Deduplication key = sha256(event_id || service || truncated_payload_hash)
- Dedupe store (configurable Redis/etcd) tracks seen keys for retention window + export retry TTL.
- Exports are retried with exponential backoff; adapters must be idempotent or use ingestion API idempotency tokens.

Export adapters and delivery guarantees
- Adapters implement a small interface: transform(envelope) -> sink_payload; deliver(sink_payload) -> receipt or transient error.
- Built-in adapters: Splunk HEC, Elastic Bulk API, Datadog logs intake, S3 archive (gzip+manifest).
- For Splunk/Elastic, we use bulk endpoints and prefer per-batch receipts; for streaming sinks, fallback to S3 snapshotting on persistent failures.

Observability and metrics
- Per-EvidenceHarvest metrics: events_captured_total, events_exported_total, events_dropped_total (with reason tags), sign_failures_total.
- Tracing: propagate trace_id from envelope; operator provides a collector-side tracing header to link operations.
- Dashboards: per-control latency percentiles (capture->export), per-sink error rates, signer queue length.

Testing and validation plan
- Unit: mapping validation, dedupe store behavior, signer (mock KMS).
- Integration: deploy operator to dev cluster with sample service, run synthetic attack/replay test to ensure dedupe and redaction work.
- Regression: ingest a curated prompt set that previously triggered false positives in mapping; ensure maps stable.
- Audit acceptance criteria: show chain-of-custody for 30-day window, verify daily manifest linking, and show RBAC enforced redaction for a scoped principal.

Operational runbooks (short)
- Key rotation: schedule via compliance runbook; rotate signerKeyRef, confirm manifest signatures for 7 days, then retire old key in KMS.
- Export failure: if adapter reports persistent 5xx > 4 attempts, operator switches flows to s3-archive sink and notifies SOC channel.
- Evidence restore: selected S3 objects can be rehydrated and replayed through the operator's test harness with the original manifest for auditors.

Security considerations
- Minimize original_payload storage by default; require explicit control binding and RBAC allowance to keep raw payloads.
- KMS keys limited to signer service; access via short-lived tokens.
- Collector sandboxing to prevent arbitrary code execution when enrichment scripts are used.

Backward compatibility notes
- We will provide a compatibility shim for existing collectors that outputs an intermediate normalizer JSON. Migration plan: enable compatibility mode per EvidenceHarvest, validate mapping with the operator's validation job, and then flip to strict mode after 7 days.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- Do we sign per-event (higher cost) or per-batch (lower cost but coarser granularity)? Proposed default: per-batch manifest + per-event hash.
- Where should dedupe store be hosted for private deployments that forbid managed Redis? Proposal: operator supports pluggable backends (etcd local, Redis, Dynamo) and an embedded option using k8s CRs for small customers.
- How many enrichment rule languages do we support? Start with Lua and WASM sandbox; evaluate policy complexity.

Next steps / proposed EPIC tasks
- EPIC-1: CRD + operator scaffolding and mapping validator (2 sprints)
- EPIC-2: Collector adapters + compatibility shim + sample service integration (3 sprints)
- EPIC-3: Signer service + manifest chain + S3 snapshot support (2 sprints)
- EPIC-4: RBAC v2 integration + redaction engine (2 sprints)
- EPIC-5: Export adapters + observability dashboards (2 sprints)

Acceptance checklist (initial)
- [ ] EvidenceHarvest CRD schema reviewed and versioned
- [ ] Operator can deploy and manage a sidecar collector and apply mapping
- [ ] Canonical envelope schema validated against three sample services
- [ ] Daily manifest signing is in place and manifests chain correctly
- [ ] At-least-once export with dedupe validated end-to-end to Splunk
- [ ] RBAC v2 redaction enforced in a scoped test case

Appendix A: Example transformed event (formatted)
{\n  "event_id": "c0a8f9b2-7f4e-4c2d-9a44-2d9b4e5f8a91",\n  "timestamp": "2025-01-10T15:22:19Z",\n  "service": "payments-service",\n  "resource": { "type": "token", "id": "tok_3f9a" },\n  "action": "token:redeem",\n  "actor": { "id": "svc-payment-worker", "principal_type": "service", "role": "worker" },\n  "result": { "status": "success", "http_status": 200 },\n  "trace_id": "4f2c9e1b-1a2b-4a2b-9c1f-8d3e6c7b9f00",\n  "control_id": ["control-PCI-DSS-10-1"],\n  "provenance": { "collector_id": "payment-sidecar-v1", "node_id": "ip-10-0-2-34" },\n  "integrity": { "algo": "SHA-256", "hash": "af3b...9d2b" },\n  "redaction": []\n}

Appendix B: Minimal mapping example (collector mapping)
- local.timestamp -> timestamp
- request_id -> trace_id
- http.status -> result.http_status
- user.id / svc.id -> actor.id
- message -> original_payload (if allowed)

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally an operator-heavy design to give central control for auditability; we expect some pushback from platform teams that prefer distributed agent-only models. Feedback welcome on operational burden and compatibility with private deployment air-gapped constraints.

-- Ava
